en.commentary: Colostrum is the supplement TikTok pushed into everyone's cart this year, and most of the 68-million-post hype skips the one number that decides whether a tub is worth your money: how much IgG you actually get per serving. That is the lens I ranked by. Transparent Labs Grass-Fed Colostrum takes the top spot because it does the boring thing brilliantly, packing a full 20 g scoop at a standardized 20% IgG and printing every gram on a third-party-tested label. When I compare cost per gram of actual immunoglobulins rather than cost per tub, it wins outright. ARMRA sits at second on the strength of its cold-chain BioPotent processing, which genuinely preserves bioactivity better than commodity spray-drying, and I rate it for people who prioritize sourcing and are happy to pay for it. WonderCow is my value champion at third, hitting a verified 30% IgG concentration from a family farm for well under a dollar a serving. The science deserves an honest caveat. A 2024 trial showed colostrum raises salivary IgA, yet a 2020 review found no significant immune-marker change in athletes, so I treat the immunity claims as promising rather than settled and lean on measurable specs instead. If you want gut and immune support with a real dose behind it, buy on IgG per serving and grass-fed sourcing, and you will land on one of my top three.

A 500 mg capsule at an unspecified IgG percentage is a different product at a different dose, and the price gap only makes sense once you do this math.

At roughly $1.67 per serving it is among the priciest options, so I recommend it to people who value bioactivity preservation above cost.

highlights.body: A verified 30% IgG concentration from a seventh-generation family farm, cold-processed and third-party checked, at well under a dollar per serving. For daily users who want potency without the boutique markup, this is the smartest money on the list.

highlights.title: Respect the science gap before you commit
highlights.body: A 2024 study found colostrum raised salivary IgA, while a 2020 review saw no significant immune-marker shift in athletes. The evidence points in a hopeful direction without closing the case, so I rank on verifiable specs like IgG content, lactoferrin, grass-fed sourcing, and third-party testing rather than on health promises.

en.commentary:
Transparent Labs stays at number one because it publishes the number that matters. IgG concentration is the active fraction in bovine colostrum, and most brands on the shelf will tell you the serving size while staying quiet about the IgG percentage inside it. Transparent Labs states its standardization and backs it with third-party certificates of analysis you can pull up before you buy.

ARMRA holds second on processing. Its cold-chain concentration protects the bioactive proteins that spray-drying at high heat degrades, and the sourcing chain from grass-fed US dairy is the most transparent in this ranking. The reason it sits behind Transparent Labs is cost per gram, which runs roughly double at typical serving sizes.

On efficacy expectations, I want to be straight with readers. The systematic review literature on bovine colostrum for gastrointestinal outcomes uses doses of 10 to 60 grams daily across four to twelve weeks. Many consumer products serve one to three grams. If you are buying colostrum for gut barrier support, the dose on the label needs to be part of the decision, and most of the value picks in the bottom half of this list are underdosed relative to the trial protocols.

WonderCow at third is where I would start for a first purchase. Whole colostrum, a stated IgG figure, and a price per serving that makes a twelve-week trial affordable rather than aspirational.

highlights.body: IgG is the immunoglobulin fraction doing the work in bovine colostrum, and a 3-gram serving standardized to 30 percent IgG delivers more active material than a 6-gram serving that never states its concentration. Transparent Labs publishes both figures alongside third-party certificates of analysis. That single disclosure is why it holds the top spot in a category where label vagueness is the norm.

highlights.body: High-heat spray drying degrades the bioactive proteins that make colostrum worth taking. ARMRA's cold-chain concentration preserves them, and its grass-fed US dairy sourcing is documented step by step. That process costs money and shows up in a price per gram roughly double the category leader, which is the entire reason it ranks second rather than first.

highlights.body: Systematic reviews of bovine colostrum for gastrointestinal outcomes use 10 to 60 grams daily over four to twelve weeks. Plenty of consumer products serve one to three grams. If gut barrier support is your goal, calculate your daily grams before you compare prices, because a cheap product at a fraction of the studied dose is the most expensive option on a per-result basis.

highlights.title: WonderCow is the sensible place to start
highlights.body: It gives you whole colostrum with a stated IgG figure and a cost per serving low enough that running a full twelve-week trial is a reasonable decision rather than a financial one.
